morning.title: Huang affair: Push for tough US line on China
morning.text: Washington: The scandal engulfing Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang could have its biggest consequences in Washington, where China hawks are seizing on the affair to push a hard line that had been put on the back burner under President Donald Trump.Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and turned it into the world's leading supplier of the processors that power artificial intelligence, admitted on Sunday to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US intelligence officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence.Also read | Nvidia's Jensen Huang should have known betterTrump, who has relied on Huang as an adviser on AI, called him "an honorable guy" and said Huang told him he had no idea the woman was a spy.Huang has spent years lobbying against curbs on sales of advanced AI chips to China, and Trump last year cleared Nvidia's H200 chips for export there over objections from hawks in both parties."China hawks in policy circles in Washington DC were quite frustrated with the decisions and really wanted to see a more aggressive approach around export controls to China," said Aalok Mehta of the Center for Strategic and International Studies."They will now see some fruits of their efforts."Many in Washington see the United States as locked in a Cold War-style race with China for technological and military dominance, and these hawks have bristled at Trump not conforming to that."What we are heading into is one of the most serious investigative efforts in a substantial period," said Kurt Campbell, a former US deputy secretary of state and co-founder of consultancy The Asia Group.Also read | Nvidia's 700,000% return faces a succession test amid Huang's China spy affairLawmakers will want to know when the government learned of the alleged links, whether the president was warned and whether the contacts shaped his China policy, Campbell said.The New York Times has reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed the allegations to Trump in May, but the president chose not to act.Nvidia committed $25 million to Trump's White House ballroom -- among the largest donations -- months after securing his approval to resume chip sales to China, The Washington Post reported. Nvidia has said the gift was independent of its business interests.Three Republican House committee chairs have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing on November 18 about his dealings with Alice Huang and Nvidia's safeguards against espionage.Not 'invincible'Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution's John L. Thornton China Center, said Republicans long feared crossing Trump.But with the party having lost control of Congress and Trump "no longer this seemingly invincible political brand," some may feel freer to break with him, Chan told AFP.That could revive the AI Overwatch Act, a bipartisan bill that would let Congress review and block licenses to export advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.The revelations have given hawks "new enthusiasm" to push through the stalled annual defense authorization bill with export control measures attached, said Emily Benson, head of strategy at Minerva Technology Futures.The key question is Trump, she said, who holds a veto that only two-thirds majorities in both chambers can override.Commerce Department staff have also pushed for new rules, including curbs on Chinese remote access to advanced AI chips, but Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick will not act without Trump's instruction, tech news outlet The Information reported.The department has already drawn scrutiny for reportedly halting a probe into Megaspeed's dealings with Nvidia.Tighter rules risk upsetting the trade truce Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping reached last year.Export control legislation seen by Beijing as targeting China "would almost certainly invite swift retaliatory action by Beijing to destabilize US supply chains," Benson said.The FBI is looking into the spying allegations, Trump said, while the Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia chips into China, NBC News reported.Megaspeed denies smuggling, and Beijing has dismissed the spying claims as smears.If wrongdoing were found and Huang forced out, "that would have huge implications for AI in the US, given that he has played such a pivotal role in pushing forward Nvidia but also the whole industry," Chan said.But even short of Huang's downfall, "Nvidia's traction within the halls of Congress and within the administration is likely to be significantly reduced or completely eliminated," Mehta said.

Anthropic is offering 801.4 million shares, while backers are selling 23.6 million shares.The figure also includes a private placement set to raise $26 billion in aggregate, to Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Broadcom Inc., Alphabet Inc.'s Google, Micron Technology Inc., Microsoft Corp., Nvidia Corp. and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the filing shows.135721915At the top of the price range, Anthropic would have a market value of about $1 trillion, based on the shares outstanding listed in the filing. Accounting for employee stock options, restricted shares and stock reserved for the company's charitable donation matching program, Anthropic would have a fully diluted value of about $1.4 trillion.Read more: Microsoft market cap beats Nvidia's for first time since June 2025Anthropic's ambitious target, including the private placement, would hit roughly $100 billion when including a so-called over-allotment option or greenshoe, Bloomberg News calculations show. That would top SpaceX's $75 billion base offering, or the $86.2 billion it raised with the greenshoe.The goal defies jitters from a sharp selloff in AI-related stocks last week, driven by expectations that politicians promising tougher regulation of data centers and related infrastructure will drive up costs and limit development of the technology.Investors are under pressure to decide whether valuations in AI reflect a plausible trajectory for a technology that many expect to transform the economy and society as a whole, or overconfidence in an investment theme that hasn't yet proven its staying power.Read more: Fed’s Christopher Waller opens door to 50-basis-point December rate hike after hot CPI The widespread adoption of Claude Code and rival tools by software developers point to the potential transformation of a wide range of professional activity, from discovering new miracle drugs to navigating complex legal and accounting rules to running a factory. It counts Novartis AG Chief Executive Officer Vas Narasimhan as one of its board members. The company's seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, are offering 3.38 million shares each in the IPO, the filing shows. The IPO is set to price on Wednesday, Nov. 18 and trade the following day, according to terms of the deal reviewed Bloomberg.Sales are surging. morning.title: Anthropic tiptoes into MS Office territory
morning.text:
Anthropic has introduced three new types of artifacts that show the company tiptoeing into the office productivity market long dominated by Microsoft and Google.

On Tuesday, the Claudefather announced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, and promised the imminent arrival of Claude Meetings. These artifact types join existing ones – Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion – to form a nascent Claude-dependent productivity suite.

Anthropic initially used the term artifacts to refer to shareable AI-based interactive tools, like dynamic charts. But the scope of the term has been stretched to cover specific artifact types, which refer to what traditionalists might take to mean files associated with specific hosted applications.

"An artifact is anything Claude makes for you that you'd put in front of someone: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard, or a small interactive tool," the company explains.

The key thing that distinguishes an artifact from a file is that users are meant to interact with artifacts through Claude, rather than storing and transferring them independently. Think of it more as a container or managed object that opens in Claude (via a sharing URL), because artifacts in fact consist of various content types – .txt, .md, .html, .jsx, .svg, .pptx, .docx, .zip, .pdf, and .mp4, among others.

Anthropic's vision of Claude as a container for other applications goes beyond artifacts. The AI biz has also expanded its interactive connectors, which turn Claude into a landlord for other software applications. Its own promotional video for the feature hammers that point home in its title: "Your apps have moved into Claude."

"Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs," Anthropic said. "Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses."

In a prior era, those would be fighting words. Tech companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft have worked for years to maintain their positions as platform landlords. Anthropic's invitation to become a Claude tenant ought to set off competition alarm bells. But perhaps with LLMs being able to re-create other people's apps on demand, there's less interest in defending app boundaries as if they were moats to keep out rivals. With AI, the call is coming from inside the house.

Alongside the rollout of Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data, Anthropic is pushing the notion that Claude is useful for people working outside of computation and mathematics, the occupational category that, according to the company's own data, accounts for a larger share of Claude usage than any other.

"Inside Anthropic, non-technical teams are starting to get as much out of Claude as our engineers," the biz insists, hauling out canned testimonials from the likes of Accenture and Datadog.

If Anthropic can demonstrate that there's an untapped market of non-coders who would welcome a Claude subscription, investors in the company's pending IPO will be glad to see it. ®

morning.title: Army Wants New Palletized Short-Range Air Defenses In Service By The End Of 2029
morning.text:
The U.S. Army is aiming to have new palletized short-range air defense systems in service before the 2029 calendar year comes to a close. The service expects these systems to be fielded on crewed and uncrewed vehicles, as well as deployed in static positions. The goal is to give combat units a more flexible array of point defenses against aerial threats, especially drone swarms, but it could also be used against ground targets.

New details about what the Army formally calls the Maneuver-Short Range Air Defense Increment 4 (M-SHORAD Inc 4) program are included in briefing slides recently released online. The presentation was originally produced for an industry day event held in Huntsville, Alabama, last month.

The overarching M-SHORAD program traces back to the late 2010s. Increment 1 produced a new mobile short-range air defense system based on the Stryker 8×8 light armored vehicle, which is now called the Sgt. Stout.

Increment 2 has been focused on operationalizing counter-drone directed energy weapons, and laser-based designs in particular. Increment 3 was originally centered on the Next Generation Short-Range Interceptor (NGSRI), a replacement for the venerable Stinger short-range surface-to-air missile. It also now covers work on the 30mm XM1223 Multi-Mode Proximity Airburst (MMPA) round for use in ground vehicles armed with the M914 cannon, like the Sgt. Stout. Development of another 30mm airburst round for use in the M230 cannons on AH-64 Apache attack helicopters falls outside of the M-SHORAD umbrella.

Increment 4 first emerged in 2025. The Army previously said it was looking for systems that could reasonably be fielded sometime between Fiscal Years 2027 and 2029. Schedule layouts in the newly released briefing slides show the goal now is to reach Initial Operational Capability (IOC) in Fiscal Year 2030. More specifically, the Army wants to hit the First Unit Equipped (FUE) milestone with a battalion-sized element in the first quarter of the 2030 fiscal cycle, which runs from October 1 to December 31 of 2029.

The Army wants the Increment 4 system to be capable of defeating a wide range of uncrewed aerial systems, from small quadcopters up to longer-range one-way-attack drones like Iran’s Shahed 136, operating individually or in swarms. It also has to be able to provide point defense against traditional helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft making attack runs on friendly ground units. The newly released briefing explicitly highlights a secondary “direct fire capability for ground targets,” as well.

No mention is made of cruise missile threats, which the Army is currently working to address through other air defense systems. However, it is possible that future M-SHORAD Increment 4 systems could be able to engage lower-end cruise missiles in certain flight profiles.

Increment 4 systems have to come in a “vehicle-agnostic” palletized format, or what the Army describes as a Self-Loading Equipment Dock (SLED), that can be readily mounted on and dismounted from light vehicles. The service has named its 4×4 Joint Light Tactical Vehicles (JLTV) and Infantry Squad Vehicles (ISV), as well as uncrewed ground vehicles (UGV), as potential hosts. The Army does not want options that require additional trailers. As palletized systems, they could also be offloaded at forward sites for static point defense.

Regardless of how they are configured, the Army wants the Increment 4 systems to “be able to operate for 72 hours independently, and semi-independently with supported force for 3-7 days,” per the recently released briefing. It also lists “C-130 loadable in normal SLED & vehicle configuration without special equipment; air droppable, sling-load and dismount capable” as key requirements.

When it comes to sensors and effectors for Increment 4, the Army continues to leave the requirements wide open for prospective vendors. The recent briefing simply notes that the systems have to feature a “reconfigurable multi-effector MEP [mission equipment package] integrating kinetic effects (e.g. missiles, direct-fire guns), and non-kinetic defeat.”

Several defense contractors – L3Harris, Leidos, Leonardo DRS, MDH Strategic Services, Moog, MSI Defense Solutions, SAIC, and the Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC), to name a few – have already publicly shown relevant designs. Versions of L3Harris’ VAMPIRE (Vehicle-Agnostic Modular Palletized ISR Rocket Equipment) systems and the Electronic Advanced Ground Launcher System (EAGLS) from MSI are already in at least limited use within the U.S. military. VAMPIRE, as well as the BRAWLR (Battery Revolving Adaptive Weapons Launcher-Reconfigurable) from SNC, are also now combat-proven as a result of service in Ukraine.

Many of the systems highlighted above feature guns like the aforementioned 30mm M914 cannon or 7.62x51mm M134 Miniguns. Stingers and AGM-114 Hellfires are commonly featured interceptors, too. SNC’s BRAWLR, which the company is also pitching for maritime applications, is notably designed to accommodate traditional anti-air missiles like the AIM-9X Sidewinder, as well.

Virtually all of the potential contenders for M-SHORAD Increment 4 incorporate anti-air optimized 70mm laser-guided Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System II (APKWS II) rockets. Originally designed as an air-to-ground weapon, APKWS II has now firmly established its place as a lower-cost counter-drone interceptor capable of being used in surface-to-air and air-to-air modes. The Ukrainian military was the first to employ these rockets in combat in the counter-drone role, but they are now in widespread U.S. military use in this capacity, too. A growing number of other countries are now moving to field APKWS II, as well as other similar laser-guided rockets, as anti-air weapons, as well.

Whatever specific types of Increment 4 systems the Army ultimately acquires, the requirement that they be palletized will offer inherent mobility and flexibility, even when not mounted on a particular host vehicle. Those attributes, in turn, could be especially beneficial for future expeditionary or distributed operations.

“Think of like a pallet or a sled that I could put in the back of any vehicle — whether it’s an ISV, a Humvee, a JLTV, or even a technical vehicle like a Toyota truck — and I can have that self-contained capability that allows the maneuver commander to have a menu of options,” then-Army Col. Marc Pelini said about Increment 4 at a panel discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention in 2025. “When I talk about [a] menu of options, I’m talking about being able to pull off a radar like an X-band radar and put a Ku-band radar on, or pull a Coyote [counter-drone interceptor] pod off and put a Stinger pod on.”

At the time, Pelini was the military deputy for the Fires Future Capability Directorate within the Army’s Transformation and Training Command (T2COM). Pelini has since been promoted to brigadier general and is now the Army’s top air defense artillery officer.

“And then, as we look at the various capabilities that are out there, from a sensing perspective, you have acoustic sensors, you have bistatic sensors, you have active radar, you have EO/IR [electro-optical/infrared] cameras. So coming up with a way that we can fuse those at the platform and at the tactical edge, and then eventually bring that up into the cloud, where we can do fusion across the entirety of the AOR [area of responsibility],” Pelini added back in 2025. “The system itself, or the pallet itself, recognizes that and automatically changes the user interface for the operator to engage those threats. So the way that we’re taking that is through an open hardware and software – really kind of a plug-and-play approach to it.”

The networking component here is particularly important as it will allow air defenders to employ Increment 4 systems in a more effective manner even if they are dispersed across a broad area. Since the systems may not all be configured in the same way, this will give operators more options to employ the effectors best suited to the incoming threats they are faced with, too. The Army currently has a network designed primarily for use with shorter-range air defense systems called Forward Area Air Defense Command and Control (FAAD C2). The service is in the process now of transitioning to the newer and more expansive Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS) network.

As mentioned at the start of this story, the kind of massed effects and fused capabilities that Increment 4 promises to this overarching architecture is seen as particularly important to helping address large volumes of drones operating in their own networked swarms.

“Right now, there is not one system that’s going to be able to defeat that swarm,” now-retired Lt. Gen. Sean Gainey, then commander of the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command (SMDC), said during a separate panel at the AUSA conference in 2025.

For a decade now, TWZ has been sounding the alarm on the drone swarm threat, and pointing to deeply layered air defense concepts with mixtures of different effectors and soft-kill systems like electronic warfare jammers as the only way to put up an effective defense. We have drawn attention to this in the past specifically within the context of larger short-range air defense gaps facing the U.S. military. The M-SHORAD effort, overall, has been at the center of Army efforts in recent years to close those gaps.

Increment 4 has always been planned to be just one layer in a still-expanding next-generation Army air defense architecture. The Army is in the process of acquiring a slew of new higher- and lower-end anti-air interceptors, as well as launchers to fire them. Laser and microwave directed energy weapons are also set to be part of this ecosystem. New and improved radars and other sensors are included in this broader air defense modernization push, too.

If the Army’s current plan for Increment 4 holds, the palletized systems will start joining its larger air defense arsenal right before the end of the decade.

morning.title: Ye olde server consolidation has made Cisco push top-of-rack switching to 100G
morning.text:
Server consolidation has led Cisco to boost the speed of top-of-rack switches to 100G.

The networking giant last week announced the catchily named N9348C8D-H2, a 1U device packing 48 100G SFP-DD ports and eight 400G QSFP-DD uplinks.

At the Cisco Live event in Melbourne, Australia, this week, Cisco’s senior veep for datacenter and internet infrastructure, Kevin Wollenweber, said one reason the company created the device is that modern servers often feature a pair of fast network interface cards.

The twin cards are needed because sixth-gen server processors from Intel and AMD offer dozens, or even hundreds, of physical processor cores and therefore generate a lot of traffic.

The density of computing power those processors provide has led chipmakers and server manufacturers to suggest replacing handfuls of machines running older, power-guzzling Xeons and Epycs with boxes running more efficient sixth-gen chips.

The Register hears it’s not uncommon to achieve 6:1 server consolidation ratios when moving from third- or fourth-generation Xeons or Epycs to current models. Users who make that move can pack many more server cores into the same rack. Power bills go down, but the quantity of data leaving a rack goes up.

Wollenweber said Cisco realized it had “tons” of switches that offer 25G ports but felt it had a gap in its range for non-AI scenarios like server consolidation that produced increased data flows.

The exec admitted that the 100G ports may be overkill for a modest collection of new servers, but argued users recognize it won’t be long before they grow into the excess capacity – perhaps as they use more agentic AI applications.

Cisco sees traffic from AI agents stressing the north-south connections that link organizations to the cloud and also driving much more east-west traffic across internal networks.

At Cisco Live, the company’s execs suggested that network upgrades are therefore an inevitable necessity.

That’s not entirely self-serving, because agents will vastly outnumber humans and constantly create traffic, compared to the flurries of network activity that happen when humans use generative AI or chatbots.

Cisco argues that deploying agents at scale will therefore only be possible on highly automated networks.

“Humans can no longer comprehend the amount of data that we actually have in a network,” Wollenweber told The Register.

Cisco’s Canvas agentic operations platform aims to at least make humans aware when their attention is needed, by detecting problems and offering to make repairs.

Joe Vaccaro, Cisco’s senior vice president and general manager for Network Platform and Assurance, told The Register he believes network administrators don’t feel threatened by suggestions from AI agents when they concern familiar, routine, low-risk tasks that IT pros are confident the agents can handle. Over time, he said, networking pros will learn to trust agents with more complex work. ®

morning.title: VMware floats new standard to make sure apps don’t break in hybrid K8s environments
morning.text:
Advocates for cloud-native software have long argued that their approach to development makes applications portable across different Kubernetes environments. But VMware argues that’s not happening across hybrid clouds, and has taken the lead in an effort to improve matters.

That effort, the new Workload Conformance Working Group in the Kubernetes community, aims to establish a shared standard for how workloads run on Kubernetes.

The group’s web page points out, “Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. Every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support,” the group asserts.

The proposed solution? “A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from.”

Prashanth Shenoy, VP of product marketing in Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) division, told The Register that standard is needed in part because applications packaged to run in public clouds don’t always run well in hybrid clouds.

That’s challenging for VMware, and other vendors of hybrid clouds like Nutanix and Red Hat, because they all sell tools to create and run a stack that users can deploy to both on-prem infrastructure and public clouds.

VMware therefore thinks it will find support for an effort to ensure that cloud-native apps run predictably and efficiently in any Kubernetes environment.

The effort to create this standard is in its very early days.

“The first step is deciding which workloads and behaviors the specification covers,” states the announcement of the working group’s formation. “The scope includes security, resilience during disruptions, resource use, networking, storage, API usage, and observability, but the group hasn’t yet agreed on specific requirements or on how to test them.

“However, one rule is already set: every requirement needs an objective test that a test binary can run, so nothing subjective goes into the specification.”

Shenoy thinks application vendors will likely support this effort because they want to package their wares once and have them run anywhere.

VM API to CNCF Sandbox

VMware this week announced another contribution to Kubernetes by moving its VM API to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox.

The CNCF, which maintains Kubernetes, is already home to KubeVirt, a tool that allows users to create and manage VMs inside a Kubernetes cluster. The VM API lets Kubernetes users create VMs that run under other hypervisors – including VMware’s own ESXi.

VMware previously integrated Kubernetes into vSphere with Kubernetes, introduced as part of vSphere 7 in 2020. Chronicling Virtzilla’s long and convoluted attempts to package and sell the container tech it acquired along with Pivotal Software would be a tedious exercise.

Suffice to say past efforts didn’t catch on, and VMware is now trying a different approach to making VMs a first class citizen of Kubernetes.

The CNCF’s interest shows this is not a vanity project for VMware, because while developers generally prefer to write for containers, operations folk often decide to run those abstractions within lightweight VMs. The two abstractions are therefore going to coexist for years to come, both for new apps and as organizations run new containerized apps alongside legacy VMs, and do so in an infrastructure-as-code world in which automated deployments are assumed.

VM API will therefore likely be a welcome addition to Kubernetes, representing another option to make life a little easier for ops and dev teams. ®

morning.title: November Patch Tuesday boasts over 1,000 bugs but only one zero-day so far
morning.text:
It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register: “Maybe we should just go home.”

“Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us.

Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one.

“It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review.

“An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.”

Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon.

Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants are undoubtedly already scanning for vulnerable versions and reverse engineering the patch for their own attack purposes. So prioritize this fix, and keep an eye on your inbox for any suspicious files.

Back-to-back months of 1K+ CVEs

Despite the second month of more than 1,000 CVEs (October had 1,474), CVE-2026-124194 is the only one under active exploitation, and none of the 1,094 are listed as publicly known. Childs says this shouldn’t give organizations “false comfort.”

“Logging back-to-back months above 1,000 CVEs proves automated bug-hunting has permanently reset patch volume,” he told The Register. “With AI making patch-diffing and exploit generation near-instant, the threat window opens the minute these updates drop.”

For defenders, this means two things, Childs added.

“What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action: patch Exchange and Domain Controllers (LDAP/Kerberos) first to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on your cloud services,” he said.

Zero-click threats

There are two zero-click threats in this month’s batch of fixes: CVE-2026-116928 and CVE-2026-119958. Both are critical, carrying 9.8 CVSS ratings, in part because they don’t require any user interaction to exploit.

CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component that could lead to remote code execution. An unauthenticated attacker could abuse this search feature in Exchange “by sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment,” Redmond warned. “Exchange automatically processes the attachment for indexing, so the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute code with the permissions of the affected processing service.”

CVE-2026-119958 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Windows' implementation of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely without user interaction. This one can be exploited by sending specially crafted LDAP requests to vulnerable systems, potentially compromising domain controllers.

Childs also counts 30 CVEs that pose a “wormable risk,” requiring zero authentication and zero user interaction over a network. All of those are listed in his blog, so prioritize fixing those as well.

And…Xbox remote code execution

And finally, for funsies, a critical flaw in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service, CVE-2026-112967, that could allow remote code execution also made this month's roundup. It's a heap-overflow vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS rating that doesn't require authentication or user interaction to exploit.

So don't take a gaming break between testing November's updates. Or, if you do, at least make sure vulnerable Windows systems running the Xbox Live Networking Service are on your patching list, too. ®

morning.title: Ring robots ready to patrol paranoids’ pads
morning.text:
If you didn't have any privacy concerns about slapping a Ring doorbell on your front door or putting Ring cameras inside, you'll love Amazon's newest offerings, which move around homes and businesses to capture views stationary cameras might miss.

The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a telescoping camera mast for automated after-hours business patrols. Both are designed to proactively patrol spaces as well as respond to alerts from connected alarm systems and Ring-connected devices.

According to Ring founder Jamie Siminoff, this is something customers actually want, as those stationary cameras just can’t quite see everywhere.

“It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have,” Siminoff said.

The consumer-focused Ring Drone Cam launches from its own charging dock that Amazon says keeps the thing “out of sight” when not in use, and when in flight is able to patrol a home by flying around pre-programmed routes to take in the sights with its 148-degree FOV, 2K camera that includes LED illumination for night patrols. Amazon says it can also respond to alerts from cameras, sensors, and alarm systems.

The Ring Rover Cam, designed with businesses in mind, is sort of like a security Roomba that sports a camera on a telescoping mast that Amazon says can be programmed to certain heights to let it see over counters, shelves, and other workplace obstacles. The Rover can also perform 360-degree scans and includes a siren, lights, and two-way audio so you can yell at intruders who aren't dissuaded by its presence. The Rover streams and records video in up to 4K while moving or patrolling and is designed to make regular patrols of businesses during off hours. It can also detect people and respond to alerts from connected Ring devices.

Of course, given that this is Ring we're talking about, these flying and free-wheeling cameras use Amazon's cloud for some processing, likely inviting privacy concerns about what footage and mapping data the company can access and retain.

The Amazon-owned security tech firm has faced a number of privacy complaints over the years, some of which have resulted in multimillion-dollar settlements. Ring agreed to pay $5.8 million in a 2023 settlement with the FTC over allegations that employees and contractors improperly accessed customers' private videos and that the company failed to adequately protect accounts against unauthorized access – just imagine the privacy concerns raised by flying robots.

More recently, the company took heat for partnering with surveillance outfit Flock Safety, a relationship which it has since canceled. Amazon/Ring also invited criticism for a Super Bowl ad earlier this year promoting a new feature called Search Party, which would remotely activate Ring cameras to search for lost pets, suggesting that Amazon had the ability, in theory, to use Ring cameras like a dystopian neighborhood surveillance network.

Another Ring feature, Familiar Faces, which uses AI-powered facial recognition to identify people captured by compatible cameras, prompted a proposed class-action lawsuit filed in June. The complaint alleges that the feature collected biometric information from visitors and passersby without their consent.

If we can’t have iRobot, we’ll do it with Ring

Amazon abandoned its efforts to buy Roomba robot-vacuum maker iRobot in 2024, blaming regulatory scrutiny for the move. The FTC, under then-chair Lina Khan, examined the deal's potential effects on competition and consumer privacy, including concerns about the information Roombas collect while mapping customers' homes. European regulators, meanwhile, raised concerns that Amazon could use its marketplace to disadvantage rival robot vacuum makers.

With this Ring move, Amazon is once again putting robots capable of mapping interior spaces into customers' hands, reviving some of the privacy questions raised during its failed iRobot acquisition.

As Amazon explains in Tuesday’s press release, both new Ring robots are powered by AI Pilot, “a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.”

To help the Ring robots understand where they're operating, the devices generate floor plans of interior spaces, according to Amazon.

“Carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan,” the company explains of the setup process. AI Pilot takes the reins in identifying the types of rooms it sees and suggests key patrol areas it should focus on, which users can add to in the Ring app.

Amazon claims that videos captured by these new flying and free-wheeling cameras will be protected by an encryption scheme it calls Throw Away the Key Encryption (TAKE). The system temporarily allows Ring's cloud services to access recordings for enabled features before the relevant encryption keys are deleted. Ring announced the scheme in August, presenting it as a way to limit access to customer recordings without sacrificing cloud-powered features.

“With TAKE, your Ring videos are protected with unique, rotating encryption keys,” Amazon explained. “A copy of the keys is temporarily held inside a secure enclave within the cloud; think of it as a sealed vault that can only provide Ring access to the key under strict, limited conditions.”

The keys, Amazon claims, are later deleted so that only users and those they allow access to can see videos, with Ring only retaining them “to power the intelligent features that you have active on your account.”

“We take privacy concerns seriously, and we believe privacy and customer control are fundamental to building products people trust,” a Ring spokesperson told The Register when asked about prior privacy concerns. “That is why customers decide where these devices go and when.”

We asked about floor plan security, but didn’t get an answer about that.

As for when those devices will be available, the Rover Cam will start shipping on December 16 at a price of about $1,000, but the Drone Cam might not ever actually make it to homes. Amazon’s announcement mentions a release date of January 27, 2027, but that’s subject to the FCC giving its blessing.

“Ring Drone Cam has not been authorized as required by the rules of the FCC,” Amazon’s release states. “This device is not, and may not be, offered for sale or lease, or sold or leased, until authorization is obtained.”

Amazon told us that the Drone Cam would still start shipping in January, luckily giving everyone a few months to figure out how to deal with this new, more mobile, invasion of privacy. ®

morning.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
morning.text:
Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows.

The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.

You had one job

Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.

morning.title: To thwart reverse engineering by agents, dev proposes blinding them
morning.text:
Now that LLMs can help analyze commercial software binaries and recreate their functionality, one software developer and student has created a project designed to make this process more difficult.

Timo Zhang's project is called Blind LLM Agents (BLA), and as its name suggests, it attempts to interfere with efforts by AI agents to scrutinize app code.

"Coding agents can reverse-engineer shipped packages, CLIs, and WASM in minutes," Zhang told The Register in an email. "Classic obfuscation was built for humans and static tools, not LLMs that reason about meaning. Blind LLM Agents is a protection layer for that threat model."

Such agents can also help developers build alternatives to existing commercial software.

Last month, Artcraft, a two-person development shop, released seven open-source apps that aim to be replacements for Adobe's commercial apps Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro. Artcraft claims these apps are "clean-room reimplementations" written from scratch in Rust using Anthropic Opus 5.5.

Setting aside the question of whether enlisting an AI model to reimplement an app really immunizes the creator from legal risk, those making apps face the possibility that someone will have an LLM probe published app binaries and reconstruct them through reverse engineering. There's in fact a framework for this, Reverse Engineer Anything (REA).

Zhang has faced some criticism on social media for creating a limited barrier to copying other people's work (which at this point might simply be the work of another LLM). But not everyone accepts that all publicly accessible binaries should be easily available for review and reuse. BLA cannot prevent committed reverse engineering efforts, but it may add a bit of friction to the process when LLMs are involved.

"It doesn't write app code — it hardens what you've already built," Zhang said. "A transform pipeline (plus MCP tools / an agent Skill) applies renaming, lane splitting, seed-derived string encryption, build polymorphism, WASM export renaming, decoys, self-seal integrity checks, and a coverage matrix that won't claim protection it can't prove. Behavior stays equivalent; recovery cost goes up."

Zhang said various evaluations like red teaming and CrackMe challenges to recover keys or flags from hardened artifacts show that BLA is effective.

"We also drive REA (a reverse-engineering agent) against those builds," he said. "Fail-to-break is the pass. CI tracks defense score, self-verifies integrity coverage, and checks functional equivalence. We raise the cost — we don't claim it is unbreakable."

The project website says as much, noting that it raises the effort for analysis and adds decoy code, but doesn't promise protection against traditional interactive reverse engineering tools like Ghidra or Frida.

Zhang said he's aware of other software projects that aim to interfere with AI, such as Poison Fountain for poisoning training data and Anubis for deterring bots and scraping. BLA, he said, is different. It's for hardening shipping code against reverse engineering and LLM-aided analysis. ®

morning.title: What happens to mathematics when AI becomes an oracle?
morning.text:
Our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning. The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. But with the rise of large language models, AI chatbots, and, soon, quantum computing, so-called "big math" is beginning to outstrip its creators entirely. What that means, and how we might adapt, is the focus of a new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World, by applied mathematicians Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend.

Strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks. He has also studied chaos theory as applied to physics, the geometry of supercoiled DNA, and the biological collective oscillators, such as swarms of synchronously flashing fireflies and crickets that chirp in unison. In 2005, Strogatz extended his study of synchronicity to the crowds that caused the wobbling of London's Millennium Bridge.

An award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The New York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. He has written four popular books: Sync (2003), The Calculus of Friendship (2009), The Joy of X (2012), and the New York Times bestseller Infinite Powers (2019).

morning.title: Barracuda’s email security gateways bitten by make-me-root vulns
morning.text:
Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security Gateway (ESG) products that, when chained, could allow the crims to run commands with root privileges.

“We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations,” the security vendor said in a late Monday night update to its earlier security advisory.

Barracuda declined to answer The Register’s questions, including one about how many organizations have been hit by attackers. A company spokesperson told us that it “worked directly” with the affected businesses “to quickly address the issue. Barracuda acted promptly to remediate the vulnerabilities, releasing patches for affected products.”

The vendor disclosed and fixed the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, last week.

CVE-2026-116606 is a 9.3 CVSS-rated, pre-authentication authorization bypass flaw in ESG. While authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have access to the administrative user interface.

As Purplecop Security founder Tausif Ahmed said on Tuesday: “If your Email Security Gateway's admin UI is open to the internet, that's the first thing I'd close today.”

CVE-2026-111560 is an 8.6-rated command-injection flaw that affects multiple Barracuda products: its ESG, load balancer (ADC), message archiver (BMA), web application firewall (WAF), WAF control center (WCC), and web security gateway (WSG).

“If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda warned on November 2. At the time, the vendor did not report any active exploitation of either.

We don’t yet know who is responsible for the attacks, or whether the intruders gained root access – but if they did, they could steal data, install backdoors, and take full control of affected systems.

These types of edge-device exploits have been used by Chinese-government spies, and in 2023 the FBI blamed PRC-linked attackers for a series of attacks that targeted Barracuda ESGs to deploy custom malware and maintain access to high-value networks. According to Mandiant, 27 percent of identified affected organizations were government entities.

So if you haven’t already: patch now. ®

morning.title: 14-year-old creates tool for AI agents to band together like a team
morning.text:
Built by a 14-year-old developer, a new tool called Autark treats AI agents as a virtual team that can work without constant prompting.

Users put tasks in an inbox, where a manager agent delegates them to other agents that carry out the work and report their results. Agents can also ask clarifying questions if tasks are too vague.

“Agents do not wait for a prompt,” Autark’s website explains. “A schedule, a timer, a new task, a message or an event wakes them up. They decide what to do, do it, and can plan their own next step.”

As one would hope from a product like this, Autark is model agnostic and can be set up to connect to OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Kimi Code through those services’ CLI tools. Local models are also supported. Your mileage may vary if you choose to use anything besides Codex or Claude Code, though, as Autark’s website mentions support for other models is built in but hasn’t been tested in a live run yet, as Autark is still under active development as an open-source tool.

Real teenage engineering

Autark is the brainchild of teenage Austrian developer Stanislaus Hees. He’s still in school, and tells The Register he’s deeply interested in AI and came up with Autark after being unhappy with existing AI tools.

“I could get help with individual tasks, but I still had to organise the work, remember what was unfinished and keep pushing it forward,” Hees said of his time using Claude Code and Codex. “I wanted a system that could take responsibility for ongoing work, not just respond to my next message.”

He developed Autark - or, more accurately, prompted AI coding tools to do it for him - to come up with a tool that could fulfill that want. You know what that means: It’s capable, but that capability also makes it dangerous.

Autark’s page on access and data makes clear what’s at risk if you give it unfettered access to a PC, and why you don’t want to let the thing run roughshod over a system.

“It can do everything,” the page explains, because “Autark does not put walls around its agents.”

There’s no sandboxing in Autark, no approval prompts, and no permission gates. It doesn’t stop agents from spending all the money they can get their hands on, deleting files, or sending unsolicited emails, either. Agents run with the privileges of the machine's user, with approval checks and permission restrictions disabled or bypassed. Even the safety limit parley that users have with Autark establishes guidelines, not rules.

“The first thing the AI asks is how far it may go,” the access page points out. “That is a question, not a technical barrier.”

That means agents given a task that conflicts with their stated limits may still attempt to carry it out. As we’ve seen in recent months, some AI agents have found ways around restrictions, instructions be damned.

“In our own live test runs, agents given a vague request reached real repositories, backups, SSH keys and .env files within minutes, and one changed the permissions of a file it had found,” the access page notes.

In other words, it’s probably best to stick Autark on a machine that doesn’t contain anything you’d want to avoid losing - even Hees admits as much.

“I would not claim that … the app is suitable for unattended access to sensitive systems,” the teen dev told us.

That’s not to say Autark lacks protections for secrets, though. Autark’s site explains that stored passwords and keys are encrypted and referred to using IDs that keep their values out of prompts. It also says its servers don't store user data, with a meeting server used to relay encrypted traffic between devices.

If you're willing to try Autark to see whether it can improve your workflows, you don't need to rely on its servers. While prepackaged apps are available from Autark’s website, it’s also fully open source and available on GitHub. Everything, even the meeting server code, is available for self-hosting and modification under an Apache open source license.

The bottom line is that this is a tool built by an ambitious young person, and it’s a tool with a lot of potential if used correctly. That correct usage is the major challenge, though, so be sure to build your own guardrails. ®

Mozilla Thunderbird email service edges closer to launch with early access
morning.text:
The Mozilla-backed Thunderbird project is getting closer to a wider launch of a hosted email service designed to complement its desktop mail app.

Now known as Thundermail (what else?), the service was originally developed under the Thunderbird Pro banner, which encompassed paid email, appointment scheduling, and file-sharing services designed to generate additional revenue for the organization.

The org has been inviting people from its Thundermail waitlist to try the service through an early-access program, and this writer just happened to be among them.

Thundermail offers a web-based email interface and can also be accessed through the Thunderbird desktop app, the Thunderbird mobile app for Android, or other compatible email clients. The Thunderbird apps remain free.

Users get an inbox with up to 15 email addresses and three custom domains, plus 30 GB of mail storage and 60 GB of send storage for Thunderbird Send, an end-to-end encrypted file-sharing and large-attachment service. That’s for starters – the org intends to offer those extra features and services at different price points.

Yes, Thundermail is a paid service, which may put off some users who are used to free email accounts offered via Gmail, Outlook.com and Proton Mail, but with the first two of those you do get served ads along with your messages.

The sign-up screens for Thundermail suggest the basic service will cost $6 per month, billed annually. This is roughly equivalent to the £55 we paid for a year on the early access program.

We asked Thunderbird when we can expect to see Thundermail officially launched and open to all comers. We will update if we get an answer. It previously said that a full launch is expected sometime in 2026.

The web-based user interface of Thundermail presents a fairly clean and uncluttered look, and could be likened to Gmail with the screen partitioned into a pane with folders on the left and a larger one to the right displaying messages.

A welcome screen introduces you to the features of Thundermail, which include the ability to work on several drafts at once, schedule delivery times for emails, create folders to arrange messages, contact lists and identities – all pretty much standard for an email system.

We haven’t really had the time to test out Thundermail a great deal since signing up, but there are no great surprises so far, and everything works pretty much the way you would expect it to.

Firefox and the Thunderbird mail client both recently moved to a fortnightly release schedule in line with Mozilla’s plans, and Thunderbird itself gained support for Microsoft’s Exchange late last year. ®

DeliverBench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Delivering Realistic Multi-Stage Professional Projects
morning.text:
arXiv:2611.03412v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM agents are judged by what they deliver, and in professional work what gets delivered is a project, not a task. A project pays off only if the whole package holds together, and one weak part can limit the value of the rest. Yet existing benchmarks mostly test agents on one task at a time, leaving a gap between the capability we measure and the outcome that makes agents useful. To address this gap, we introduce DeliverBench, which tests whether agents can carry a project from brief to final delivery. Reconstructed from real materials with 13 domain experts, its 11 projects span settings such as financial due diligence, legal contract drafting, and drug safety reporting. They comprise 150 subtasks, with 2-15 subsequent releases of new materials and client feedback per project. Later subtasks build on the agent's own earlier deliverables, so unresolved errors can carry into downstream work. Expert rubrics assess each subtask submission and the final delivery package. Across seven model-harness systems, the best scores 65.0/100 on final delivery and passes 50.0% of subtasks at a 90-point threshold. Together, these results suggest that task-level capability does not simply compose into delivery; delivery also depends on keeping the work coherent as it evolves.

morning.title: ClinFusion: A Vision-Centric Multimodal LLM System for Holistic Medical Understanding
morning.text:
arXiv:2607.24743v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) hold immense potential to revolutionize clinical practice, yet deploying them in the medical domain is fundamentally a vision-centric challenge: models must absorb knowledge from heterogeneous 2D and 3D medical images, and evaluation protocols must align with radiologists' clinical practice and provide an accurate, fine-grained and factualness-driven assessment. In this paper, we introduce ClinFusion, a vision-centric MLLM designed for holistic medical understanding that systematically addresses these limitations. We propose a compositional and cascaded vision encoder architecture featuring a Cascade Spatial-Aware Locality Fusion operator that unifies diverse 2D and native 3D medical image understanding within a fused encoder. We further introduce a vision-grounded evaluation framework, including MedIF-Bench for instruction-following assessment and a region-of-interest-grounded method for clinically aligned and factualness-driven report generation evaluation. We show that ClinFusion sets a new state-of-the-art across a comprehensive suite of 2D and 3D multimodal medical benchmarks---spanning visual question answering, report generation, and instruction following---as well as textual medical tasks, outperforming leading open-source medical MLLMs (\textit{e.g.}, Hulu-Med, Lingshu) on 20 out of 24 benchmarks and demonstrating multimodal capabilities better than powerful proprietary models such as GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Flash on 13 out of 16 benchmarks, and can be further augmented with agentic tool use for retrieval-augmented and tool-assisted clinical workflows. A blinded evaluation by board-certified radiologists confirms that ClinFusion produces the highest-ranked reports, and validates our RoI-grounded metric as achieving the strongest correlation with expert judgment among all automatic evaluation metrics examined.

morning.title: What Does a Harness Repair? Four Preregistered Studies Around a Longevity-Tuned Language Model
morning.text:
arXiv:2610.05533v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A harness search around a frozen longevity-tuned 1.7B model reported a rescue. An audit traced its gain to rows the start left unparsed and found that the caller sent reference answers as assistant turns; replication through the same pipeline missed this defect. We preregistered four studies and report every endpoint. In the first two, thinking off raised test accuracy over capped thinking in 7 of 12 cells, mainly by parsing rows the cap left unparsed, and was not meaningfully worse than a rescue in 7 of 9 small-model test cells. Replication reproduced an injected defect's distortion in 9 of 20 evaluable cases. At 14B, two GEPA harnesses beat thinking off by 34 test points but were not detectably above the strongest constant label. In the third study, GEPA beat the constant on FPB (confirmatory), thinking off was not meaningfully worse than any BoolQ harness, and 3 of 4 MMLU-Pro searches kept their seed; the fourth comparison was inconclusive on test. On exploratory Autocast, harnesses were within 0.7 points of the constant and gave one label in 93.1% to 96.8% of parsed answers on test. On the prediction tasks (14B mortality, Autocast) the harnesses ended near the constant label. The fourth study varied search-set skew and objective on CREAK and resolved Manifold questions. All its results are descriptive because render hashes were not committed before the first replication call (D001). Minority-recall estimates were lower at 80:20 than at 50:50 in all four test cells. The balanced objective and re-selection from each search's pool had higher minority- and lower majority-recall estimates in all four cells. Five of their eight minority-recall intervals included zero, as did all eight balanced-accuracy contrast intervals. This does not show that skew explains the earlier collapse.

morning.title: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks
morning.text:
arXiv:2611.01728v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.

morning.title: Scene-Adaptive Readout and Decoding in Diffusion Driving VLAs
morning.text:
arXiv:2611.02076v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Diffusion driving vision-language-action models repeatedly execute the backbone at every denoising stage, incurring substantial inference cost, while it remains unclear whether all scenes require the same decoding computation. To distinguish when a trajectory becomes readable from how much further refinement it requires, we analyze trajectory readout across network depth and decoding progress. We identify a depth-decoding dissociation in which late-layer representations already support useful trajectory readout after the first forward sweep, whereas early-layer representations benefit more from continued decoding. We further find that both the preferred readout layer and decoding depth vary across scenes. Based on these observations, we propose a scene-adaptive readout and decoding framework. A scene-conditioned readout MoE adaptively weights and combines trajectory predictions from layer-specific late-layer representations after a single backbone sweep, while an adaptive decoding policy applies additional native refinement only when required by the scene. We evaluate our framework on two diffusion driving VLAs across the Waymo E2E and nuScenes benchmarks. Our method improves validation RFS by up to 0.56 while also improving test performance, and achieves an end-to-end speedup of up to $6.0\times$ on Waymo E2E, while consistently reducing trajectory error on nuScenes. These results demonstrate that scene-level readout and decoding allocation improves planning quality while avoiding unnecessary decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/SARD

morning.title: Army chief to move into new Shaurya Bhavan from South Block, Navy chief to Sena Bhavan
morning.text:
New Delhi: Army chief General Dhiraj Seth, along with his seven Principal Staff Officers (PSOs) and the Vice Chief, will move lock, stock and barrel from South Block to the Army’s new headquarters, Shaurya Bhavan, in Delhi Cantonment by the end of this month.
Navy chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan will also move out of South Block, along with his Vice Chief and Principal Staff Officers, to Sena Bhavan, located just behind South Block.
While the Navy already has Nausena Bhavan in Delhi Cantonment, which was inaugurated in 2024, its new headquarters were originally planned to come up next to the DRDO headquarters. However, the Navy has been asked to relinquish the site as part of the Central government’s redevelopment plan.
Incidentally, the office of the Director General of Military Operations (DGMO) and the Army’s war room will also be shifted, sources said.
It is not clear where the Navy’s war room will be relocated, given the extensive infrastructure and technological support required to operate it.
South Block has traditionally housed the headquarters of both the Army and the Navy, with their respective chiefs operating from there.
Officers serving under the Department of Military Affairs, including the Director General of Defence Intelligence Agency (DG DIA), will also move out of South Block.
The Defence Ministry has temporarily shifted to Kartavya Bhavan 2 and will permanently move to Kartavya Bhavan 6 and 7 once the buildings are completed.
Currently, only the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) has an office at Kartavya Bhavan 2. This means the Army chief will have to travel from Delhi Cantonment to meet the Defence Minister and other senior functionaries at Kartavya Bhavan 2 until the new buildings are ready.
Kartavya Bhavan 6 and 7 will also accommodate additional offices for the service chiefs.

morning.title: Trump admin ‘withholding’ approval for Europe-funded Patriot missiles for Ukraine—WaPo report
morning.text:
New Delhi: The Trump administration has withheld approval for sending crucial Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine, according to a report by The Washington Post report published Tuesday, leaving Kyiv vulnerable to ongoing Russian missile and drone strikes.
This delay comes amid US President Donald Trump’s recent public criticism of Ukraine and a marked change in his stance toward Russia.
Unlike previous debates in Washington over multi-billion-dollar military aid packages funded by US taxpayers, the current bottleneck involves weapons that have already been bought and paid for. European allies and the Ukrainian government have utilised billions in cleared funds through NATO frameworks to secure the interceptors. However, the transfers remain subject to US authorisation.
The bottleneck can be traced to US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, who has neither formally rejected the transfers nor taken the necessary steps to authorise them. By withholding his signature on essential agreement documents, Hegseth has stalled deliveries without openly announcing a policy shift.
The weapons are being purchased through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) framework, which allows European allies to fund the purchase of American military supplies for Kyiv without drawing on US taxpayer funds. Multiple countries including Germany, Norway and the Netherlands have pooled financial resources to purchase American military equipment.
However, since Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors are manufactured in the US by RTX and Lockheed Martin, international partners cannot transfer them without Washington’s approval. This applies to both new factory orders and re-export requests from European inventories.
The delay comes as Ukraine faces a critical shortage of Patriot interceptors.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy noted that monthly deliveries of the missiles from the US have been throttled to approximately 12 units, or a fourth of the prior supply rate. A Ukrainian official told The Washington Post last Thursday that Kyiv’s reserves had dwindled to just “a couple” of functional interceptors, leaving its air defences critically strained.
Global availability of Patriot interceptors has also come under pressure from ongoing military engagements in West Asia. The Pentagon has signalled to Congress its intention to divert roughly $750 million in partner-provided PURL funding away from Kyiv to replenish depleted US stockpiles of THAAD and Patriot systems.
On Monday, Zelenskyy put out a video appeal to US senators where he talked about the deliberate slowdown of missile shipments being leveraged to discourage Ukrainian drone strikes against Russian oil-refining infrastructure.
These tensions are further compounded by efforts in Washington to soften specific sanctions on Russian fuel exports, highlighting a rift between American energy objectives and Ukraine’s defensive strategy.
Seeking to resolve the deadlock, Zelenskyy announced on his official Telegram channel Tuesday that he had held what he described as a “substantive” and “constructive” call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Beyond the stalled Patriot deliveries, the dialogue touched upon wider security concerns, including a suspension of American early-warning tracking intelligence and bandwidth restrictions affecting Starlink and military Starshield satellite communications.
However, the State Department lacks the regulatory authority to override Pentagon export restrictions. While Rubio kept communication channels open, Washington has continued to press Kyiv towards diplomatic negotiations with Moscow.
The operational impact of the delays has been compounded by Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Recent strikes severed electricity access for over 500,000 households across the Kyiv region, underscoring the consequences of Ukraine’s strained air-defence capabilities.
The delays have also prompted political opposition on Capitol Hill, where congressional leaders are questioning the administration’s handling of the situation. During an official press interaction Monday, Representative Rosa DeLauro, Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Committee, criticised Hegseth’s administrative hold, arguing that using bureaucratic procedures to stall shipments undermines confidence among global allies.
This legislative backlash contrasts with Trump’s position on continued aid to Kyiv.
The US President has reiterated his scepticism towards ongoing assistance to Ukraine, telling news outlets that Ukraine has “given nothing to us”, while asserting that withholding weapons transfers could provide leverage to push both nations towards peace talks.
Ashwin Shekhar is an alum of ThePrint School of Journalism, currently interning with ThePrint.

morning.title: Pulp packaging to mega defence orders: SMPP’s rise, CBI probe & looming threat of a ban
morning.text:
New Delhi: From a pulp-based packaging firm in Punjab’s Sangrur to a major supplier to India’s armed forces, SMPP’s transformation into a defence manufacturing company has been remarkable.
But following the arrest of its CEO in a corruption case involving a state-owned ammunition manufacturer, the company now faces the prospect of suspension and a possible ban on business with the defence ministry, its main customer.
Sources in the defence and security establishment told ThePrint that the defence ministry will follow due process in dealing with corruption-related allegations, adding that the Department of Defence Production (DDP) was seized of the matter.
On Tuesday, the CBI arrested Ashish Kansal, CEO and director of SMPP Limited, along with Anil Kumar, a senior executive director at state-owned Munitions India Limited (MIL), in connection with an alleged corruption case.
Suspension kicks in, ban could follow
Under the Defence Procurement Manual (DPM) 2025, the competent authority can suspend a company pending an inquiry under specified circumstances, including when a complaint is referred to an investigating agency or the defence ministry receives information about a criminal investigation. The ministry would examine the relevant records and the company’s response before deciding on further action. A proposed debarment across government departments is also subject to the applicable procedures and safeguards.
The competent authority would then decide whether the grounds warrant lifting the suspension or banning dealings with the company altogether.
The applicable provisions distinguish between interim suspension and a ban, which can have far-reaching consequences for a defence supplier. The final decision under the relevant suspension and banning provisions rests with the defence minister.
The order of suspension of business dealings is to be issued for a period the competent authority deems fit, though the period of suspension shall not ordinarily exceed one year. A review of the order or suspension of business dealings is to be undertaken within six months of the issue of such an order and before expiry of the period specified therein.
The suspension of an entity may be extended beyond the period of one year, on the order of the competent authority for subsequent periods of six months each.
The total period of suspension shall not exceed the maximum period of banning of business dealings for the same cause of action. An order of suspension of business dealings, however, shall result in immediate ineligibility of the entity from participating in future bids.
No RFP (request for proposal) is to be issued to such an entity. Further, any ongoing procurement, where L1 (lowest bidder) determination is yet to be done, is to move forward after excluding the bid involving an entity with which business dealings are suspended.
According to the process, banning of business dealings with an entity may be ordered by the competent authority on acceptance of misconduct by the entity or establishment of such misconduct by a competent court/tribunal/authority. Banning of business dealings with an entity can be ordered by the competent authority on receipt of information regarding filing of charge sheet in a court of law by CBI or any other investigating agency.
From packaging to defence manufacturing
SMPP was founded in 1985 by Dr Shiv Chand Kansal, a chemical engineer with a PhD from IIT Bombay. The company, originally incorporated as SM Pulp Packaging Private Limited, started out as a pulp-based packaging business.
Under the leadership of the Kansal family, it gradually moved into defence manufacturing, building capabilities in specialised materials and protection systems. In the 1990s, SMPP began manufacturing semi-combustible cartridge cases for 120 mm and 125 mm ammunition. This marked its entry into defence-related manufacturing and materials technology.
It subsequently obtained licences to manufacture bullet-resistant jackets, vehicle armour, and protective systems for aircraft and helicopters. It subsequently expanded its portfolio to include helmets, armour plates, shields and other protection equipment.
Its first major breakthrough in the Indian defence market came in 2018, when it secured a contract to supply 1,86,000 bullet-resistant jackets to the Army.
At the time, SMPP was a relatively little-known player in the defence sector. Its use of boron carbide ceramics, an extremely hard material used in advanced armour systems, helped reduce the weight of personal protection while providing multi-hit protection against hard steel-core rounds. But the contract also brought scrutiny.
During the trial phase, SMPP had used fabric and boron carbide plates sourced from the US. After securing the contract, it switched to Chinese material, triggering questions about the change and its cost implications. The Economic Times first reported on the issue in 2019. SMPP’s defence was that it made the change after obtaining necessary approvals from the Army. The company subsequently expanded its defence business, supplying different types of armour and protective equipment, including helmets, to the armed forces.

Ammunition & drones: an expanding portfolio
In 2021, SMPP incorporated SMPP Ammunition Private Limited as a subsidiary and set up a manufacturing plant at Nalagarh in Himachal Pradesh.
The subsidiary was subsequently issued an arms licence by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) to manufacture ammunition in several calibres, including 125 mm, 120 mm, 155 mm, 130 mm, 105 mm, 81 mm, 40 mm and 30 mm.
SMPP also expanded its overseas business, exporting products to more than 23 countries across Europe and Asia, according to the company.
It entered into a partnership with Rheinmetall Denel Munition, a joint venture between Germany’s Rheinmetall Waffe Munition GmbH (RWM) and South Africa’s state-owned Denel, for large-calibre ammunition. Rheinmetall, the German defence group, has separately faced restrictions on defence dealings in India following a corruption investigation by the CBI.
SMPP has also ventured into unmanned systems. In June this year, it delivered 106 jet-powered kamikaze drones under an emergency procurement programme of the Indian Army, as part of efforts to accelerate military modernisation following Operation Sindoor.
The drones, marketed as Peacekeeper and also known as Agniveg, are designed to operate in GPS-denied environments. They are reported to have a range of 180 km and a top speed of around 450 km per hour.
Sources in the defence and security establishment told ThePrint that the platform was originally developed by Belarusian company KB Indela, which partnered with SMPP.
Under the transfer-of-technology (ToT) arrangement, SMPP localised the warhead component of the drones. The understanding is that ToT would be phased, with further localisation, including manufacture of the jet engine, as order volumes increase. The defence manufacturer has also offered a next-generation version capable of reaching speeds of around 750 km per hour.
As far as SMPP’s future outlook is concerned, drones, protective gears and ammunition manufacturing would have remained the core areas.
Profits soar as business expands
SMPP’s financial performance has strengthened alongside its expansion into defence manufacturing.
Revenue rose to Rs 622.57 crore in FY2024-25 from Rs 376.92 crore in FY2021-22, an increase of 65 percent.
Net profit nearly doubled over the same period, rising from Rs 87.74 crore to Rs 174.61 crore.
The company’s reported growth in profits outpaced revenue growth, pointing to a significant improvement in its earnings over the period.
Its defence business, spanning personal protection, ammunition components and newer unmanned systems, has expanded considerably.
SMPP has also faced procurement-related scrutiny overseas.
The company, which established a joint venture in the Philippines, was blacklisted by the Philippine National Police (PNP) in September 2025 over alleged failure to fulfil contractual obligations relating to a contract for all-purpose vests. The disqualification was reported to run for one year, until September 2026. It remains unclear whether the blacklisting has since been lifted or extended.
